Brazil’s Metals & Mining Industry Recovers After Credit Freeze

A severe credit freeze that disrupted Brazil’s Metals & Mining sector over the past month ended this week, with major firms, including Vale SA, resuming normal operations after a government-brokered resolution. The crisis, triggered by the abrupt withdrawal of short-term lending by domestic banks amid concerns about global metal price volatility, left companies struggling to meet payrolls and fund ongoing extraction projects.

The freeze began in early May, when rising fears over global oversupply of iron ore and nickel led several Brazilian lenders to tighten credit requirements for mining companies. As a result, firms found themselves unable to refinance maturing debts or secure working capital. The National Mining Trade Association (ANM) estimates that at least R$8.7 billion in project financing was suspended across the sector over a three-week period.

“Many operations came to a near standstill,” said ANM President Guilherme Tavares. “Without access to credit, companies could not pay suppliers, contractors, or employees, putting tens of thousands of mining jobs at risk.”

Vale SA, the country’s largest iron ore producer, was among those worst affected. The company confirmed that three of its major mineral processing plants in Minas Gerais state were forced to scale back output by as much as 40% in late May due to the cash squeeze. “We faced unprecedented challenges in maintaining our supply chain,” said Vale SA’s Chief Financial Officer, Mariana Lopes. “Our priority was to protect our workforce and maintain essential operations, but the situation became critical.”

Smaller firms, such as the Belo Horizonte-based Mineração Serra Verde, reported similar difficulties. “We were days away from missing payroll and halting our exploration activities,” said CEO Ricardo Ferreira.

The crisis abated after the Ministry of Mines and Energy, in coordination with the Central Bank, announced a temporary credit support package last Thursday. The government-backed facility guarantees up to R$5 billion in new lending to metals and mining companies on preferential terms, provided the funds are used to maintain employment and resume suspended projects.

Industry leaders welcomed the intervention. “This was a necessary step to restore liquidity and confidence,” said mining union representative Sandra Coutinho. “Our members are relieved to be returning to work.”

With the new credit lines in place, Vale SA and other producers said they have restarted previously halted operations, and are working to restore production to pre-crisis levels. While analysts warn that market conditions remain fragile, the sector appears to have avoided the worst-case scenario of widespread bankruptcies and prolonged shutdowns.
